messages.subject: How to define my own distance measure in MatchIt?
messages.subject_clean: How to define my own distance measure in MatchIt?
messages.body_plain:
Hello MatchIt community,

I am relatively new to MatchIt and I am now working on a causal inference study with MatchIt.
I my study, I would like to use my own distance measure for matching.

I have read the manual which mentions that MatchIt allows users to use a vector of user-made distance measure as the input.
Can anyone give me an example for this? 

Given a data set with 1000 items, I have computed a distance matrix (1000*1000). And what should I do in the next step?

Thanks you very much!

Best,
Gang

messages.subject: Re: How to define my own distance measure in MatchIt?
messages.subject_clean: How to define my own distance measure in MatchIt?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Gang,
MatchIt doesn't take the distance matrix (it will create it itself from the vector you send it).  So I'm not sure it will be appropriate for what you are trying to do.  If you want to send MatchIt a vector of "distances" (e.g., propensity scores you have estimated yourself) you use a command like:

m.out.fr1 <- matchit(treat ~ var1 + var2 + var3, data=dta, distance=dta$pscore)

I know the optmatch package does take a distance matrix as input so you could try that.

Liz

Dear MatchIt- Team,

I am currently using the "MatchIt" package in R to do some nonparametric 
preprocessing of my data (school achievement data of students in 
Germany). Afterwards I want to estimate the ATT of a certain 
intervention with the matched data (using Zelig). After reading several 
of your papers (which was really a pleasure!) I wonder, if there is any 
possibility to obtain the Abadie - Imbens SE, t- statistics & p- value 
of the ATT via the summary command in Zelig. By default, only the point 
estimate, its standard error and the 95- confidence interval is printed. 
Do you know if and how this could be achieved?

Thank you in advance and kind regards,

Aleksander Kocaj

messages.subject: Design vs. analysis
messages.body_plain:
Aleksander Kocaj <a.kocaj-Zg63vc6wD9n31zTM6d8ziw at public.gmane.org> wrote:

> I wonder, if there is any possibility to obtain the Abadie - Imbens SE, t- statistics & p- value of the ATT via the summary command in Zelig.

On Sat, Oct 13, 2012 at 6:30 PM, Kosuke Imai <kimai-uX/v2g6dJhCyum0STUha2w at public.gmane.org> wrote:
> Unfortunately, that option is not currently available in Zelig.

An underlying philosophy in MatchIt is that the first job of analysing
observational data is to get the design right. Once you have a good
design, you go about analysing that cleaned-up design asif that data
came from an experiment. This is a simple and attractive perspective.

I happened to discuss this with Alberto Abadie a few weeks ago and his
argument lay in two parts. The design that comes out of any matching
process involves a statistical estimate of which are the matched
units, which units are deleted, etc. In general, we can't ignore that
dimension. Specifically, he pointed out a paper coauthored by him
where the bootstrap doesn't work well in these situations owing to
non-differentiability of the likelihood function across choices of
different permutations. (Abadie and Imbens in their Econometrica 2008
paper show that classical bootstrap schemes fail to provide correct
inference for  K-nearest neighbour (KNN) matching estimators of
average causal effects.)

In short, he said (a) You can't ignore the origins of your design and
proceed on analysis and (b) You can't just bootstrap your way to
happiness.

I am not an expert in this field and I am aware the literature is
moving fast. E.g. http://ftp.iza.org/dp5361.pdf in 2010 seem to have
figured out how to do bootstrap
inference works for a 1:K nearest neighbour matching estimator.
Elizabeth Stuart's beautiful survey article had pointed out that oddly
enough, in many situations, taking the sampling perspective on the
matching process gives you improved precision.

As an applied researcher I am delighted to be in the world of Matchit,
where painstaking care is applied in the design stage. I have no doubt
in my mind that this is a superior world when compared with the old
econometrics. I am curious what the wise men on this list think about
these questions. And, if a journal referee insists that I should do
alternative inference procedures such as Abadie/Imbens, what would one
do?

-- 
Ajay Shah
ajayshah-zJnVPX2nTqnYtjvyW6yDsg at public.gmane.org

messages.subject: Re: Design vs. analysis
messages.body_plain:
Abadie and Imbens are appealing to a different theory of uncertainty than
most matchit-based approaches do.  Within that theory, the only uncertainty
is due to repeated simple random sampling from the population and so for
each sample, you will likely wind up with a different matched set and as
such the matching process itself needs to be part of the standard errors or
confidence intervals.  That led them to study bootstrapping+matching and to
produce other very useful asymptotic results.

That is a perfectly fine theory, within its particular uncertainty
framework.  However, there are other frameworks, and picking one is
essentially an arbitrary theoretical choice.  Almost by definition, we have
no empirical evidence to distinguish whether the one data set we see comes
from a multiverse generated by repeated simple random sampling, repeated
stratified random sampling, stochastic potential outcomes, random treatment
assignment, etc., etc.  Each leads to different estimators and conclusions,
including ones that makes matchit easy to use.

Here's a paper<http://gking.harvard.edu/publications/how-coarsening-simplifies-matching-based-causal-inference-theory>
we
wrote that lays out with some specificity an alternative theory of
uncertainty that is much easier (and more matchit-friendly) by allowing you
to match and then condition on the matched sample when computing SE's and
CIs via the usual parametric regression or other approach, ignoring the
matching method.  It also allows finite sample inference.  There are plenty
of others that could be constructed too, each of which would lead to
different estimation techniques.

So if you like the Abadie and Imbens simple random sampling theory of where
randomness and uncertainty comes from, and are ok with asymptotic results,
then you should clearly go to their estimation techniques.  If you are
willing to go with other theories of uncertainty, then you can make other
choices.

So I think this is something you can probably explain to your reviewers.
 but if not, there's an article in the current issue of Science indicating
that if you get your paper rejected from your first choice journal and
accepted at a lower-ranked journal, the number of citations to your paper
will be higher;  I only read the abstract however and haven't checked their
theory of uncertainty!

Gary

messages.subject: Genetic Matching with MatchIt
messages.body_plain:
Dear MatchIt Team,

I am using the MatchIt package to implement genetic matching. As a result, the
achieved balance on all covariates is better compared to other matching methods
except for the distance measure (derived through logistic regression,using the
command: distance ="logit"). I could fix that issue using the Matching- Package
(J.S. Sehkon) by defining, on which variables I would like to achieve balance on
via the "BalanceMatrix" option. I included the distance measure in that matrix.
Is there an option to define such a matrix with MatchIt? Otherwise, the balance
on the distance measure is not satisfying after matching with matchit(stand.
mean difference > 0.15). What I need is a command to tell the genetic algorithm
to achieve balance on all covariates AND the combined distance measure.

Thank you for your help in advance and kind regards,

Aleks

messages.subject: Re: Genetic Matching with MatchIt
messages.body_plain:
An approximated solution to this problem:
1) Estimate a propensity score before Matching (e.g. via glm, family =binomial)
2) Merge the resulting vector(data$glm <- glm$fitted) to the dataframe
3) Include this new variable in the Matching formula (matchit(Treatment~glm+...)
I tried it that way and achieved better balance on the distance measure without
affecting balance on all single covariates. It worked for all 15 imputations of
my dataframe, although I do not know if this approach conflicts with the
"silently added propensity score to X when method=='genetic".

Best,

aleks
